chem-permanent-marker: Permanent markers write in a solvent-based ink: pigments are dissolved or suspended in alcohol and other solvents that dissolve into the writing surface — plastic, glass, metal — so the color bonds with the material rather than sitting on top. Once the solvent evaporates, a resin film locks the pigment in place, making it hard to remove without another solvent. That's why alcohol removes permanent ink: it redissolves the resin.
chem-dry-erase-marker: Dry-erase markers use a release chemistry that permanent markers lack: the ink contains a slippery silicone or release agent along with pigment and solvent, so the pigment sits on the whiteboard surface in a low-friction film instead of bonding to it. The solvent evaporates and the resin film stays put until friction — a dry eraser — lifts it off. The trick is a polymer that doesn't wet the board.
chem-sticky-notes: Sticky notes stick because of a weak adhesive applied in microdots: a low-tack, pressure-sensitive polymer that grips just enough to hold paper to paper without damaging either surface. The adhesive is applied in tiny beads, so only part of the note actually contacts the surface. The balance — tacky enough to stick, weak enough to peel — comes from tuning the polymer's softness and how it wets surfaces.
chem-superglue-chemistry: Superglue is cyanoacrylate, a monomer that polymerizes in the presence of water — and there's always a film of moisture on surfaces, which is why it sets almost instantly. The water triggers the molecules to link into long polymer chains, and the reaction bonds whatever is touching. It cures fastest in a thin gap with slight pressure; thick blobs stay liquid in the middle. It also bonds skin instantly for the same reason.
chem-glue-stick: A glue stick is a solid polymer adhesive: typically a blend of water-soluble polymers like PVP (polyvinylpyrrolidone) that dissolve in water and grip paper fibers as they dry. The stick format works because the polymer is solid at room temperature but softens and transfers onto paper with friction. As the water evaporates, the polymer dries into a flexible film. That's also why glue-stick bonds are washable — water redissolves the film.
chem-duct-tape: Duct tape is a pressure-sensitive adhesive sandwich: a polyethylene film coated with a rubber-based adhesive layer that flows into microscopic surface roughness under pressure, creating a bond without heat or water. The adhesive's tack comes from being soft enough to wet surfaces but elastic enough to resist peeling. The fabric reinforcement gives it strength, and the adhesive layer can be peeled cleanly — the chemistry of strong-but-removable.
chem-velcro-chemistry: Velcro is a mechanical fastener with no glue: one side is thousands of nylon hooks and the other loops, and pressing them together makes the hooks catch the loops. The nylon is a strong, flexible polymer that withstands repeated bending. The 'chemistry' is in the material choice — nylon's toughness and elasticity — but the grip is pure geometry. It's the same principle as burs clinging to animal fur, which inspired its invention.
chem-zipper-history: The zipper is a purely mechanical fastener — interlocking teeth — but its history is chemistry-adjacent: early versions used brass teeth that corroded and jammed, until nickel-plated steel and later nylon coils solved it. The slider geometry that interlocks teeth was perfected over decades. Nylon coil zippers, introduced in the 1950s, are self-lubricating and flexible. The modern zipper is an engineering triumph where materials science made the mechanics work.
chem-velcro-space-age: Velcro's fame as a space-age fastener is partly myth: NASA didn't invent it, but astronauts did use it to keep objects from floating in zero gravity. The hook-and-loop system works purely mechanically — nylon hooks gripping nylon loops — with no adhesive chemistry involved. What made it space-worthy was material choice: nylon withstands vacuum, temperature swings, and doesn't outgas. Its grip comes from thousands of tiny mechanical catches, not chemical bonds.
chem-memory-foam: Memory foam is a viscoelastic polyurethane: a polymer foam with a carefully tuned glass-transition temperature near room temperature, so it's soft and squishy at body warmth but slow to spring back. When you press it, the heat and pressure soften the polymer, letting it conform; when you remove pressure, it recovers slowly. The 'memory' is the polymer chains relaxing back to their original shape over seconds — pure polymer physics.
chem-mythbusters-tv: Mythbusters tested the chemistry behind dozens of urban legends: whether cola dissolves teeth, whether adding salt to a pot makes water boil faster, whether Mentos in Diet Coke erupts. Many myths are about real chemistry — the Mentos eruption is carbon dioxide released by nucleation, and salt does raise water's boiling point, just not meaningfully at kitchen amounts. The show popularized the scientific method, turning chemistry claims into testable experiments.
chem-mentos-coke: The Mentos-and-Coke eruption is nucleation chemistry: the candy's rough, pitted surface gives dissolved carbon dioxide thousands of places to form bubbles at once, and the sudden burst of gas violently expels the liquid. It's not a chemical reaction — neither the candy nor the soda is transformed. The candy's density also makes it sink fast, and the gum arabic and gelatin help stabilize the foam. Pure physical chemistry, spectacularly demonstrated.
chem-diet-coke-mentos: Diet Coke erupts higher than regular Coke with Mentos because of surface chemistry: diet soda's artificial sweeteners lower the liquid's surface tension, so the foam that forms is lighter and weaker, and the bubbles expand faster. The Mentos surface provides nucleation sites that release dissolved CO2 in a cascade. Regular soda's sugar thickens the liquid, damping the eruption. Same reaction, different fluid physics — which is why the diet version wins the fountain race.
chem-elephant-toothpaste: Elephant toothpaste is decomposition made dramatic: hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen, and the catalyst — potassium iodide or yeast — speeds the reaction so fast that oxygen erupts. Dish soap traps the gas in thick foam, and food coloring streaks it like toothpaste. It's the same reaction that whitens teeth or bleaches hair, scaled up. The foam is mostly harmless oxygen and soap — safe to touch after the reaction finishes.
chem-invisible-ink: Invisible ink is chemistry with a reveal: lemon juice or milk are acids that weaken paper fibers, so heating the page chars the treated spots darker than the surrounding paper — the message appears as if by magic. Other inks reveal under UV light or with a chemical developer like iodine or iron salts. The principle is a substance invisible on paper that reacts to heat, light, or another chemical to become visible.
chem-milk-and-dish-soap: The milk-and-dish-soap experiment shows surface tension: food coloring floats on milk's surface, then a drop of soap breaks the surface film — the soap molecules wedge between the fat and water, dragging the color around in dramatic swirls. The movement is the soap chasing the fat molecules, and it stops when the soap spreads evenly. It's a visible lesson in surfactants, the chemistry behind cleaning.
chem-lava-lamp-chemistry: A lava lamp is liquid-liquid density chemistry: a dense, waxy fluid sits at the bottom of a clear liquid, and the heat from the lamp expands the wax until it becomes less dense than the water around it — then it floats up, cools, and sinks again. The wax's density curve is tuned so a slight temperature change flips it. The blobs are the wax cycling through this density inversion, powered purely by heat convection.
chem-density-layering: Density layering works because liquids with different densities stack like floors: oil floats on water, water floats on corn syrup, and each added liquid settles into its own level. The order is set by density, not volume — pour heavy liquids first and lighter ones on top. It's the same principle that lets a submarine float or sink. The layers stay separate because the liquids don't mix, which comes down to molecular polarity.
chem-rainbow-density-tower: A rainbow density tower stacks colored sugar-water solutions of different concentrations: more sugar means denser liquid, so the sweetest layer sinks to the bottom and the least sweet floats on top. Each layer is dyed a different color, creating a suspended rainbow. The trick works because sugar dissolves without changing volume much, so the layers stay distinct and won't mix unless shaken — a liquid density gradient you can see.
chem-slime-chemistry: Slime forms when polyvinyl alcohol (in glue) crosslinks with borate ions: the borax provides boron that temporarily links the glue's polymer chains together, turning runny glue into a stretchy, gooey network. The crosslinks break and reform as you play, which is why slime stretches and flows. More borax means more crosslinks and stiffer slime; more water means runnier. It's polymer chemistry you can hold in your hand.
chem-oobleck: Oobleck — cornstarch and water — is a non-Newtonian fluid: under slow pressure the starch particles slide past each other and it flows like liquid, but a sudden force jams the particles together and it stiffens like a solid. The cornstarch grains are irregular and water-lubricated, so they lock up under impact. You can run across it, but stand still and you sink. It's stress-thickening chemistry at the particle level.
chem-non-newtonian-fluids: Non-Newtonian fluids disobey the simple rule that viscosity is constant: ketchup thins when shaken, quicksand and oobleck thicken under impact, and paint thins under a brush but holds its shape on the wall. The behavior comes from how particles or polymers rearrange under stress — long molecules align and flow, or suspended particles jam together. Cornstarch, ketchup, blood, and quicksand are all examples of the same family of fluid physics.
chem-ketchup-viscosity: Ketchup is a shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: at rest, its tomato solids and thickeners form a network that holds the bottle shut, but shaking or squeezing breaks that network, letting it pour. The longer molecules and particles align under stress, the more fluid it becomes — which is why it suddenly gushes. It's a yield-stress fluid: nothing moves until the force passes a threshold, then everything flows at once.
chem-quicksand: Quicksand is sand suspended in water, and it behaves like a non-Newtonian fluid: the grains are loosely packed and waterlogged, so a sudden movement causes them to shift and liquefy, and you sink. The trick to escaping is moving slowly — gentle movement lets the sand grains settle back into a packed, supportive state. Quicksand is denser than the human body, so it can't actually swallow you whole; you float, like in salt water.
chem-cornstarch-nonnewtonian: Cornstarch in water is the classic shear-thickening fluid: slow pressure lets the starch particles slide past each other so the mix flows, but a fast impact jams them together into a rigid mass. The result is a fluid that hardens the harder you hit it — punch oobleck and it feels like a solid, yet your hand sinks in slowly. Particle jamming, not chemical change, does the work.
chem-rock-candy: Rock candy grows by controlled crystallization: a supersaturated sugar solution — more sugar dissolved in hot water than can stay dissolved cold — slowly cools, and sugar molecules deposit onto a seed string, building large crystals over days. Each molecule slots into the growing lattice, which is why the crystals are geometric. The slow evaporation concentrates the solution further, feeding crystal growth. It's the same process that grows geodes and snowflakes.
chem-salt-crystals-experiment: Salt crystals grow when a saturated salt solution slowly evaporates: as water leaves, the solution becomes supersaturated, and sodium chloride molecules begin locking into cubic lattices on a seed surface. Because salt's crystal habit is cubic, the crystals form perfect little cubes and hopper shapes. The slower the evaporation, the larger and more regular the crystals — a visible lesson in how ionic compounds assemble.
chem-borax-crystals: Borax crystals grow from supersaturation: hot water holds more borax than cold, so as a saturated solution cools, the excess borax deposits onto a suspended pipe cleaner or string, forming white, spiky clusters. Each crystal is sodium borate locking into its lattice, and the pipe cleaner's fuzz gives thousands of nucleation sites for growth. Slow cooling produces larger crystals; fast cooling makes many small ones.
chem-sugar-glass: Sugar glass is a supersaturated solid solution: sugar and corn syrup are heated until molten, then cooled into a brittle, transparent solid that shatters like glass — perfect for movie breakaway bottles and windows. Unlike crystal glass, it has no crystalline structure; it's an amorphous solid of sugar molecules. The corn syrup prevents crystallization during cooling, keeping it clear instead of turning cloudy and grainy.
